concept.name: JWT Validation Pitfalls

relationships.description: Connects JWT Validation Pitfalls to api security oauth2 in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Stateless JSON Web Tokens fail catastrophically when verifiers trust header fields (`alg`, `kid`, `jku`), skip audience/issuer checks, or confuse asymmetric public keys with HMAC secrets.
spark.keyTakeaway: Never let an untrusted token dictate how it is verified: enforce a strict server-side algorithm allowlist, pin trusted JWKS endpoints, and validate `iss`, `aud`, and `exp` on every request.

concept.whyItMatters: JWTs are self-describing—they carry their own algorithm (`alg`), key ID (`kid`), and key URL (`jku`) inside an unauthenticated Base64URL header. Naive verification libraries that obey those header hints let attackers forge arbitrary admin tokens without knowing any secret.
whenToUse: Stateless service-to-service or API-gateway authentication using short-lived (`5–15 min`) RS256/ES256 tokens issued by an OIDC provider (Auth0, Okta, Keycloak, Cognito).
Cross-domain SSO (OAuth 2.0 / OIDC `id_token`) where resource servers verify signatures locally via cached JWKS public keys.
whenNotToUse: Browser session tokens requiring instant global logout or immediate revocation upon permission downgrade (prefer opaque reference tokens + Redis/DB lookup).
Storing large user profiles or sensitive PII inside unencrypted JWS tokens (JWT payloads are Base64URL-encoded, not encrypted—anyone can decode them).
keyPoints: `alg: none` & Key Confusion (CVE-2015-9235): trusting the token's `alg` header lets an attacker strip the signature (`alg: none`) or re-sign a token with HS256 using your public RSA key as the HMAC secret.
`kid` Injection & Path Traversal: interpolating the `kid` header into a SQL query (`SELECT key FROM keys WHERE id = '$kid'`) or file path (`../../dev/null`) enables trivial signature bypass.
`jku` / `x5u` SSRF & Key Spoofing: fetching public keys from a URL embedded in the JWT header lets an attacker host their own JWKS and sign valid-looking tokens.
Missing `aud` (Audience) & `iss` (Issuer) Checks: a valid JWT issued for `billing-api` or a third-party tenant can be replayed against `admin-api` if only the signature and `exp` are checked.
Clock Skew & Revocation Gap: generous `exp` windows (24h+) or unbounded clock leeway undermine security; keep access tokens short (`300–900s`) and bound leeway to `<= 60s`.

examples.title: RS256-to-HS256 Key Confusion Bypass
examples.scenario: A Node.js API calls `jwt.verify(token, publicKey)` without passing `{ algorithms: ['RS256'] }`. An attacker downloads the public `.pem` from `/.well-known/jwks.json`.
examples.outcome: The attacker mints `{ sub: 'admin', role: 'superuser' }`, sets `alg: 'HS256'`, and signs it with the public PEM bytes as the HMAC secret. Because the server's `verify()` obeys the header's `alg`, it validates the forged admin token until `algorithms: ['RS256']` is enforced.

examples.title: Cross-Service Token Replay via Missing `aud` Check
examples.scenario: Two microservices (`service-a` and `service-b`) share the same OIDC Identity Provider, and `service-b` only validates the RS256 signature and `exp`.
examples.outcome: A compromised token scoped for `aud: 'service-a'` (with `scope: 'read:profile'`) is replayed against `service-b`, granting unintended access. Adding strict `audience: 'https://api.example.com/service-b'` validation blocks the replay.

tradeOffs.pro: Local signature verification via cached JWKS eliminates a network hop to the IdP on every API call (~0.1 ms CPU vs ~15 ms RPC).
tradeOffs.con: Compromised or logged-out JWTs remain valid until `exp` unless you add a stateful `jti` denylist in Redis.

tradeOffs.pro: Caching JWKS for 5–15 minutes prevents IdP rate-limiting and protects against `kid`-miss DoS attacks.
tradeOffs.con: Emergency key revocation requires an out-of-band cache invalidation or short TTLs; unknown `kid` lookups must be rate-limited.

tradeOffs.pro: Asymmetric signing ensures resource servers only hold public keys, so a compromised API node cannot mint tokens.
tradeOffs.con: RS256/ES256 verification is ~10x slower in CPU cycles than HMAC-SHA256 (though still sub-millisecond).

failureModes.name: JWKS Cache-Busting DoS
failureModes.description: An attacker sends 10,000 requests with random `kid` values; the API gateway synchronously fetches `/.well-known/jwks.json` on every cache miss, taking down the IdP.
failureModes.mitigation: Rate-limit JWKS refreshes (e.g., max once per 60 seconds) and reject unknown `kid`s locally between refreshes.

failureModes.name: Critical Header (`crit`) Bypass
failureModes.description: A library ignores unknown `crit` extensions per RFC 7515 §4.1.11, bypassing custom policy enforcement expected by the issuer.
failureModes.mitigation: Use RFC 8725-compliant libraries (e.g., `nimbus-jose-jwt`, `jose`, `PyJWT >= 2.8`) that reject unsupported `crit` headers by default.

failureModes.name: PII Leakage in Browser Logs & Referer Headers
failureModes.description: Developers place JWTs in query strings (`?token=eyJ...`) or store sensitive claims in unencrypted JWS payloads.
failureModes.mitigation: Always transmit JWTs in `Authorization: Bearer` headers, never URLs, and use JWE if payloads contain confidential fields.

failureModes.name: Symmetric Secret Brute-Forcing
failureModes.description: An HS256 token signed with a weak secret like `supersecret123` is cracked offline in minutes using `hashcat`.
failureModes.mitigation: Prefer ES256/RS256; if HS256 is required, use at least 256 bits of CSPRNG entropy.

commonMistakes: Calling `jwt.decode()` (which only Base64-decodes without verifying the signature) instead of `jwt.verify()`.
Omitting the explicit `algorithms` allowlist (`['ES256']` or `['RS256']`), leaving the verifier vulnerable to `alg: none` or HS256 key confusion.
Storing JWTs in `localStorage` where any XSS script can exfiltrate them, instead of `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax` cookies or BFF patterns.
Accepting tokens without checking `iss` (Issuer) and `aud` (Audience), allowing cross-tenant or cross-service token replay.
Setting multi-day `exp` lifetimes on access tokens without a `jti` revocation check or refresh-token rotation.

sections.content:
## The idea

A JSON Web Signature (JWS, RFC 7515) consists of three Base64URL-encoded segments: `header.payload.signature`. The trap is that **the header is attacker-controlled input** until the signature is verified. Because the header tells a naive parser *which* algorithm (`alg`) and *which* key (`kid`, `jku`, `x5u`) to use, any verifier that blindly follows header instructions hands control of the verification state machine to the caller.

RFC 8725 (JWT Best Current Practices) establishes one golden rule: **server policy overrides token headers**. The verifier must dictate the allowed algorithms (`ES256`, `RS256`, `EdDSA`), pin the trusted issuer's JWKS URI out-of-band, and enforce semantic claim checks (`iss`, `aud`, `exp`, `nbf`) before any downstream business logic reads `sub` or `roles`.

## Concrete walkthrough

Walk through a hardened verification pipeline in an Envoy / API Gateway + Resource Service:

1. **Parse & Reject**: Extract the `Bearer` token. Reject tokens exceeding 8 KB, tokens with `!= 3` dot-separated parts, or headers containing `jku`, `x5u`, or unsupported `crit` extensions.
2. **Algorithm Allowlist**: Read `header.alg`. If `alg` is not in the server's pinned list (e.g., `["RS256", "ES256"]`), reject immediately with `401 Unauthorized`—blocking `alg: none` and `HS256` key confusion.
3. **Pinned JWKS Lookup**: Look up `header.kid` in the in-memory JWKS cache populated solely from the pre-configured `https://auth.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json`. Also verify the JWK's `use: "sig"` and `alg` match.
4. **Cryptographic Verify**: Verify the signature over `ASCII(header + '.' + payload)` using constant-time comparison.
5. **Semantic Claims**: Assert `iss == "https://auth.example.com/"`, `"api://orders" in aud`, `now < exp + 30s`, and `now >= nbf - 30s`. Optionally check `jti` against a Redis revocation set for high-risk actions.

sections.content:
## The key confusion & `kid` injection mechanics

Why did `CVE-2015-9235` affect so many libraries? Because early APIs had a single `verify(token, secretOrKey)` signature:

- When `alg` was `RS256`, `secretOrKey` was treated as an RSA public key.
- When an attacker changed `alg` to `HS256`, the exact same function passed the RSA public key string (`-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----...`) into `HMAC_SHA256(key, data)`.

Since RSA public keys are *public* (exposed at `/.well-known/jwks.json`), anyone could compute a valid HMAC tag. Similarly, if `kid` is used to build a filesystem path (`keys/${kid}.pem`), setting `kid: "../../../dev/null"` causes the verifier to read an empty string `""` as the HMAC secret, letting the attacker sign tokens with an empty key.

sections.eyebrow: 04 / Common JWT pitfalls and RFC 8725 defenses
sections.content:
## Common JWT pitfalls and RFC 8725 defenses

| Pitfall | Attack Vector | Impact | RFC 8725 Defense |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`alg: none`** | Strip signature, set `alg: "none"` | Full authentication bypass | Reject `none`; require explicit `algorithms: ['RS256']` |
| **RS256 -> HS256** | Sign with public PEM as HMAC secret | Arbitrary token forgery | Separate key types; pin `alg` per key in JWKS |
| **`kid` Traversal / SQLi** | `kid: "../../dev/null"` or `' UNION...` | Known/empty key verification | Validate `kid` as strict UUID/alphanumeric regex |
| **`jku` / `x5u` Spoofing** | Point `jku` to attacker-controlled JSON | Self-signed valid tokens | Ignore `jku`/`x5u`; pin IdP JWKS URL server-side |
| **Missing `aud` / `iss`** | Replay token from Service A to Service B | Cross-service privilege escalation | Assert exact `iss` and `aud` match on every endpoint |

## Failure modes

- **Subtle `aud` array mismatch**: RFC 7519 allows `aud` to be either a JSON string or an array of strings; naive string equality (`claims.aud == myService`) fails or breaks when an IdP emits an array.
- **Type confusion (`typ` header)**: Accepting an OAuth `at+jwt` access token where an OIDC `id_token` is expected (or vice versa) can bypass authorization scopes. Enforce explicit `typ` checks where supported.
- **Revocation blind spot**: Relying solely on 24-hour JWTs means an employee whose account is disabled at 09:05 retains API access until 09:05 the next day.

## Hybrid stateless + stateful patterns

For high-security systems, combine short-lived JWTs with minimal state:

1. **Short access tokens (`exp = 300s`) + Refresh Token Rotation**: Clients refresh silently; revoking the refresh token in the database caps exposure to 5 minutes.
2. **Phantom Token Pattern (API Gateway)**: The browser/mobile client holds an opaque reference token; the edge API Gateway exchanges it once (cached in Redis for 30–60s) for an internal signed JWT before forwarding to microservices. Internal services get fast stateless JWTs while external clients never see internal claims or user PII.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Pass an explicit `algorithms` allowlist (`['ES256']` or `['RS256']`) to every `verify()` call—never rely on defaults.
- [ ] Enforce `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, and `nbf` validation with `<= 60s` clock skew leeway.
- [ ] Ignore `jku`, `x5u`, and `jwk` embedded headers; load keys strictly from a pinned, rate-limited JWKS cache.
- [ ] Sanitize `kid` against `[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+` before any cache or map lookup.
- [ ] Keep access token `exp` <= 15 minutes and back critical mutations with a `jti` revocation check or opaque gateway token.

interviewProblems.title: JWT Validation Pitfalls
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on JWT Validation Pitfalls. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Stateless JSON Web Tokens fail catastrophically when verifiers trust header fields (`alg`, `kid`, `jku`), skip audience/issuer checks, or confuse asymmetric public keys with HMAC secrets.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Pinned JWKS Cache applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Resource Service.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Resource Service experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Rate-limit JWKS refreshes (e.g., max once per 60 seconds) and reject unknown `kid`s locally between refreshes.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Never let an untrusted token dictate how it is verified: enforce a strict server-side algorithm allowlist, pin trusted JWKS endpoints, and validate `iss`, `aud`, and `exp` on every request.
Avoid trap: Calling `jwt.decode()` (which only Base64-decodes without verifying the signature) instead of `jwt.verify()`.
Avoid trap: Omitting the explicit `algorithms` allowlist (`['ES256']` or `['RS256']`), leaving the verifier vulnerable to `alg: none` or HS256 key confusion.
When to reach for it: Stateless service-to-service or API-gateway authentication using short-lived (`5–15 min`) RS256/ES256 tokens issued by an OIDC provider (Auth0, Okta, Keycloak, Cognito).
When to reach for it: Cross-domain SSO (OAuth 2.0 / OIDC `id_token`) where resource servers verify signatures locally via cached JWKS public keys.

putItTogether.title: Putting Jwt Validation Pitfalls Together
putItTogether.summary: Never let an untrusted token dictate how it is verified: enforce a strict server-side algorithm allowlist, pin trusted JWKS endpoints, and validate `iss`, `aud`, and `exp` on every request.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Jwt Validation Pitfalls before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: The attacker mints `{ sub: 'admin', role: 'superuser' }`, sets `alg: 'HS256'`, and signs it with the public PEM bytes as the HMAC secret. Because the server's `verify()` obeys the header's `alg`, it validates the forged admin token until `algorithms: ['RS256']` is enforced.
